meta.ogDescription: The famous one-liner isn’t in any translation of Heraclitus — it’s a modern paraphrase of his idea that everything flows.

answer.label: Not a real Heraclitus quotation — a modern paraphrase
answer.authorDates: c. 540 – c. 480 BC · Pre-Socratic Greek philosopher of Ephesus
answer.sourceLine: The neat one-liner appears in no standard translation of Heraclitus; it is a modern English paraphrase. His surviving work centers on change and flux — the genuine fragment is about a river — but the crisp aphorism “the only constant in life is change” is a later coinage, and scholars caution that even the “everything is in flux” reading was partly imposed on him by Plato and later interpreters ↗.

source.excerpt: On those stepping into rivers staying the same other and other waters flow. — Heraclitus, Fragment B12
trail: The exact phrasings “change is the only constant” and “the only constant is change” are grouped by Wikiquote ↗ among statements that “paraphrase or extend upon his famous assertions … in ways which arguably diverge from valid translation.”
Philosopher Keith Begley notes that “there is no surviving quotation that says ‘Life is flux’ or that all things are in radical flux,” calling the popular picture a later imposition on Heraclitus ↗.

The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy ↗ reports that scholars treat B12 as “the one and only river fragment,” and that the radical-flux reading “is no longer the only reading of Heraclitus advocated by scholars.”
source.excerptNote: The genuine surviving fragment closest to the popular saying. Note it does not claim “everything changes” — it describes a river that stays the same river precisely because its waters change. The tidy aphorism “the only constant is change” does not appear here or anywhere in the corpus.
source.rightsNote: The ancient Greek text is public domain, but the displayed English wording is an anonymous modern paraphrase, not a specific dated translation. With no identifiable translator and no evidence of pre-1931 documentation for this exact sentence, we assert no copyright status for the phrasing.

author.name: Heraclitus
author.heading: About Heraclitus
author.metaLine: c. 540 – c. 480 BCE · Pre-Socratic Greek philosopher of Ephesus
author.bio: Heraclitus of Ephesus was a Pre-Socratic Greek philosopher active around 500 BCE, known in antiquity as “the obscure” for his riddling aphorisms. His thought centers on the unity of opposites and on change: things persist through, and because of, transformation — captured in his image of a river whose waters are always different. He wrote a single book, now lost, that survives only in scattered quotations by later authors.

copyAttribution: "The only constant in life is change" is a modern paraphrase, not a quotation from Heraclitus — it appears in no standard translation of his work.

misattribution.heading: The wording is modern; the label is ancient
misattribution.intro: This is the classic “right spirit, wrong quote” case: the sentiment echoes Heraclitus, but the polished sentence is a modern invention pinned onto his name.

items.why: No standard translation of Heraclitus contains “the only constant in life is change.” Wikiquote ↗ files it among phrasings that “diverge from valid translation,” and popular pieces that credit it to him cite no primary source ↗.

items.who: Partly Plato and later interpreters, not Heraclitus himself
items.why: The “everything is in flux” picture was shaped by Plato and his follower Cratylus ↗; his genuine river fragment stresses that some things stay the same by changing, not that all is chaos.

misattribution.truthLine: The idea of change is genuinely Heraclitean, but — as Keith Begley notes ↗ — “there is no surviving quotation” giving this aphorism; the tidy one-liner is a modern coinage.

context.heading: Why this one sticks to Heraclitus
lead: Heraclitus really is the philosopher of change — his surviving fragments turn on flux, opposites, and a river you cannot step into twice. So when a crisp modern motivational line about change needs a distinguished ancient sponsor, his name is the obvious fit, and the attribution feels right even though the sentence is not his.

The irony scholars point out is that Heraclitus’ actual river fragment argues the opposite of pure flux: the river stays one river precisely because its waters keep changing. The popular slogan flattens that subtlety into a bumper sticker.
detailsBody: His book is lost; roughly a hundred short fragments survive as quotations in later authors such as Plato, Aristotle, Plotinus and Diogenes Laertius.
The genuine river fragment (B12) reads, in a literal rendering, “On those stepping into rivers staying the same other and other waters flow.”
The Greek tag “panta rhei” (“everything flows”) that often stands in for his view was itself a later characterization, not a verbatim quotation from his book.
